summary: In April 1978 the communist People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan seized power in a coup. Its radical reforms and harsh repression provoked uprisings across the country, and its two factions fought each other. In December 1979 the Soviet Union sent its 40th Army into Afghanistan, killed the party leader Hafizullah Amin and installed Babrak Karmal. Soviet and Afghan government forces held the cities and main roads, but could not defeat the mujahideen, Islamic resistance groups operating from the mountains and from refugee camps in Pakistan. The United States, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, China and others armed and funded the resistance, with Pakistan's intelligence service distributing the aid. After repeated offensives, mounting losses and the arrival of US Stinger anti-aircraft missiles, Mikhail Gorbachev's government sought a way out. Under the Geneva Accords of April 1988 Soviet troops withdrew, the last leaving on 15 February 1989. Najibullah's government survived until 1992, when civil war among the mujahideen followed.
casualties: An estimated 1 to 3 million Afghans died, most of them civilians, along with 14,453 Soviet soldiers by official count (other estimates reach 26,000); about 5 million Afghans fled abroad.

sources.title: Office of the Historian, US State Dept: The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan and the U.S. Response, 1978–1980

brief.hook: Afghanistan's new communist rulers faced revolt across the country; in December 1979 the Soviet army marched in to save them.

sides.who: The Soviet Union's 40th Army and the forces of Afghanistan's communist government: its army, police and secret police
Afghan Islamic resistance groups, based in the mountains and in Pakistan, armed by the United States, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, China and others

brief.resultLine: Under the Geneva Accords of April 1988 the Soviet army pulled out, its last soldiers leaving on 15 February 1989; the Afghan civil war went on.

strategies.name: Guerrilla war from the mountains
strategies.text: The mujahideen avoided set battles. They ambushed convoys on the mountain roads and slipped back to valleys like the Panjshir or to camps in Pakistan, so the Soviets held the cities but never the countryside.

strategies.name: Scorched earth
strategies.text: Soviet aircraft levelled villages, wrecked irrigation channels and sowed millions of mines to empty the countryside that fed the rebels. Millions of Afghans fled, but the resistance survived.

strategies.name: Foreign arms and the Stinger
strategies.text: American and Saudi money, passed out by Pakistan's intelligence service, rose to hundreds of millions of dollars a year. From 1986 shoulder-fired Stinger missiles let rebels shoot down helicopters, challenging Soviet control of the sky.

impact: Perhaps one to three million Afghans died, and about five million fled abroad, mostly to Pakistan and Iran.
The costly, unwinnable war is widely seen as one cause of the Soviet Union's collapse in 1991.
Afghanistan slid into civil war among the mujahideen, from which the Taliban rose to power in the 1990s.
The Taliban later gave Osama bin Laden a base, setting the stage for the American war of 2001.

sources.title: Office of the Historian, US State Department: The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan and the U.S. Response, 1978–1980

details: The communist government that took power in April 1978 pushed land and social reforms by force and arrested and executed thousands of opponents. On 15 March 1979 a popular revolt broke out in the western city of Herat, joined by mutinous soldiers of the army's 17th Division. Communist officials and some Soviet advisers were killed. Government forces retook the city on 20 March and bombed it; estimates of the dead range from 3,000 to 25,000. Taraki asked Moscow for troops, but the Soviet leadership at first refused.

Rivalry within the ruling party ended in September 1979 when Prime Minister Hafizullah Amin overthrew President Nur Muhammad Taraki, who was killed soon afterwards. Amin intensified the repression, while rebellion spread and the army suffered mass desertions and mutinies. Soviet leaders distrusted him, feared that Afghanistan might be lost to Islamist rebels or turn to the West, and began planning an intervention.

On 24–25 December 1979 Soviet forces began crossing the Amu Darya from the Uzbek SSR and flying troops into Kabul and the Bagram air base. Ground columns moved south along the main highways, and within weeks tens of thousands of Soviet soldiers were in the country. Moscow presented the operation as assistance requested by the Afghan government under a 1978 friendship treaty.

On the evening of 27 December Soviet special forces stormed the Tajbeg Palace outside Kabul in Operation Storm-333, killing Amin, while other units seized key buildings in the capital. Babrak Karmal, leader of the party's rival Parcham faction, was installed as head of government. The UN General Assembly condemned the intervention on 14 January 1980 by 104 votes to 18, and the United States responded with sanctions and a boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics.

The Panjshir Valley north of Kabul, close to the Salang highway that carried Soviet supplies, was the base of Ahmad Shah Massoud, the most effective mujahideen commander. In April 1980 Soviet and Afghan troops launched the first of nine major offensives there. Each time the guerrillas withdrew into the side valleys and mountains, and returned once the troops left. Further offensives followed in August and December 1980 and September 1981, with the same result.

On 16 May 1982 about 12,000 Soviet and Afghan troops attacked the Panjshir with hundreds of armoured vehicles and over 100 helicopters, landing some 4,200 airborne troops behind Massoud's defences. They occupied much of the valley floor and set up garrisons, but most of the mujahideen escaped and kept fighting from the heights. Villages were destroyed and much of the valley's population fled.

After repeated failed offensives, Massoud negotiated the first Soviet–mujahideen ceasefire directly with a Soviet military intelligence officer in January 1983. Soviet forces withdrew from most of the Panjshir, leaving a small garrison, and Massoud used the pause to extend his influence and organisation into neighbouring regions. The truce did not cover the Salang Pass, where fighting went on. Other resistance leaders criticised the deal, and full-scale fighting in the valley resumed in 1984.

In the eastern province of Paktia, near the Pakistani border, mujahideen forces surrounded the garrison town of Khost in July 1983. Its defenders could be supplied only by air for years. The siege symbolised the war's pattern: the government held the towns, while the resistance controlled much of the countryside and the routes to its bases and supply depots in Pakistan.

When the 1983 truce collapsed, Soviet commanders launched the seventh and largest Panjshir offensive on 19 April 1984, preceded by heavy bombing that included high-altitude raids. Massoud, forewarned, had evacuated many civilians and fighters. Troops fought through the valley into September, but the mujahideen again survived, and Soviet forces evacuated the valley in September. Two more offensives followed, in September 1984 and June 1985; the last Soviet and Afghan troops left the lower Panjshir in June 1988.

Mikhail Gorbachev, Soviet leader from 1985, wanted to end a costly war. On 4 May 1986 Karmal was replaced as party leader by Mohammad Najibullah, former head of the secret police. In the same year the United States began supplying the mujahideen with Stinger shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles, about 2,300 in all, through its covert programme Operation Cyclone, which made Soviet helicopters and aircraft far more vulnerable.

At the start of 1987 Najibullah announced a policy of national reconciliation, offering a ceasefire, power-sharing and an end to the party's monopoly in an effort to win over opponents and prepare for Soviet withdrawal. The main mujahideen parties, based in Peshawar in Pakistan, rejected the offer. Fighting continued, and the government relied ever more on militias paid with Soviet money.

From 19 November 1987 to 10 January 1988 Soviet and Afghan forces fought to reopen the road from Gardez to besieged Khost, cut for months by the mujahideen. Soviet troops entered Khost on 30 December and convoys brought in supplies. It was one of the last big Soviet operations; once the main force pulled back, the mujahideen closed the road again.

On 14 April 1988 Afghanistan and Pakistan signed the Geneva Accords at the United Nations in Geneva, with the Soviet Union and the United States as guarantors. They set a timetable for Soviet withdrawal, which began on 15 May. Half the troops had left by mid-August. The mujahideen were not party to the accords, and outside powers kept arming both sides.

The second phase of the withdrawal ran from November 1988, and on 15 February 1989 the last Soviet column crossed the Amu Darya bridge into the Uzbek SSR, led by the 40th Army's commander, General Boris Gromov. About 620,000 Soviet personnel had served in Afghanistan. The war had damaged the Soviet economy and the army's prestige, and it is often counted among the causes of the Soviet Union's collapse.

Expecting Najibullah's government to collapse, mujahideen groups backed by Pakistan's intelligence service attacked the eastern city of Jalalabad on 5 March 1989, joined by Arab volunteers. Government forces held the city, and fighting lasted until the end of June. The defeat divided the resistance and showed that the Afghan army could fight without Soviet troops. Najibullah's government survived until April 1992.
